Sun Rui <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/secure/ViewProfile.jspa?name=sunrui> created an issue

SparkR <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR> /  <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-125> SPARKR-125 <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-125>
Get the iterator of the parent RDD before launching a R worker process in compute() of RRDD/PairwiseRRDD <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-125>
Issue Type:    Improvement
Assignee:   Sun Rui <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/secure/ViewProfile.jspa?name=sunrui>
Components:   Internals
Created:   11/Oct/14 1:00 AM
Priority:    Major
Reporter:   Sun Rui <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/secure/ViewProfile.jspa?name=sunrui>

Currently, in compute() of RRDD/PairwiseRRDD, iterator() of the parent RDD is called after a R worker process is launched. This causes larger memory consumption because current RDD's R worker process will wait for parent RDD's computation and can do nothing before parent RDD's computation returns. If the parent RDD is an RRDD, then both R worker process of current and parent RRDD co-exist, which makes no sense.

Optimization can be done by getting the iterator of the parent RDD before launching a R worker process.

Yes, I put that link down because I suspect except DataBricks guys and those follow the news announcements, quite some may be unaware of that project exists (They just open source it months after their initial presentation). There may be something to 'share' in terms of higher level interface.

Went to quite a number of Berkeley R and SF R meetups and notice there is a quite some "information /cultural gap" between software engineers and R Statisticians (not Machine Learning):
most of the experienced R guys (refer to "they" hereafter) are unaware of R on Spark
those who are aware deeply believe they have to use Java/Python to use Spark.
they find ML libraries from Python and Java only contain the basic algorithms; and is insufficient for their daily work
those who do use, some are concern that Libraries from other ecosystem is not rigorously 'Peer-reviewed'
lots of latest methods are published in R and with the paper;
R, to them, goes from data munging to publishing (for internal meetings quickly - cycle ranging from days/1-2 week time frame), Public facing data viz, leave that to software developers. So another disincentive to learn other language.
want to keep their R way of doing thing, and very importantly able to use the other R packages.
unlike other ecosystems, there are SO MANY STYLES depending on what R packages to use (for examples data.frame, plyr, dplyr, sqldf, data.table etc), Learn another language not top of their list.
most of their time is spent on exploring new and tweaking existing model, they rely on sampling to do their work to proceed and literately quickly. Processing all data is not top of their list.
they are behind programmers ways of working (like git or even source control etc). Only recently aware of considering making R packages etc

currently SparkR is really slow. I ran the wordcount example with 3.2G data on a 3-slave spark cluster (16 logical CPUs and 48G memory per node) and it took 3.8 hours to complete. After I enabled map-side reduction, the time was shortened to 1.6 hours. While a scala version of wordcount only takes 17 seconds on the same dataset. You can try the following steps to see if the performance can be improved:
1. Pull the latest code in which map-side reduction in reduceByKey() has been enabled;
2. set driver memory using SPARK_MEM variable;
3. Modify the wordcount source code:
  sc <- sparkR.init(args[[1]], "RwordCount", , sparkEnvir=list(spark.executor.memory="3g"))
4. Modify the wordcount source code to increase the reducer number for reduceByKey():
  counts <- reduceByKey(wordCount, "+", 10L)

Labels:   MLlib
Priority:    Major
Reporter:   Oscar Olmedo <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/secure/ViewProfile.jspa?name=OscarO>

Having a LabeledPoint is the first step to using MLlib

Perhaps the data is comma separated with the last column as the label 1 or 0
e.g.
3.4,6.0,7.1,3.5,7.3,1
4.3,2.2,3.3,9.0,4.5,1
4.4,6.7,5.5,7.8,2.3,0
...

readPartition=function(part)
{ part = strsplit(part, ",", fixed = T)[[1]] arr=c(part[length(part)],part[1:(length(part)-1)]) label=part[length(part)] vector=part[1:(length(part)-1)] return(list(label=label,vector=vector)) }

rdd <- textFile(sc,datafile)
points <- LabeledPoints(cache(lapply(rdd, readPartition)))

LabeledPoints() return a LabeledPoints RDD that can be passed to MLlib.

In order to use MLlib library the build.sbt must be modified by adding
"org.apache.spark" % "spark-mllib_2.10" % "1.1.0"
to the libraryDependencies

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for benchmarking -- I think there are a couple of things here that affect performance, and can be improved.

- Number of reducers: The default value gives bad performance and we should set the default number based on number of partitions in the previous RDD. Hao Lin actually did this for `distinct`, but we need to do it for reduceByKey as well.

- Benchmark programs: One of the big bottlenecks in the word count example is that the performance of computing hashCode on strings is very slow. It would be great to also run Logistic Regression to get another data point which doesn't use string-keys for shuffle. (FYI The hashCode performance improvement is being tracked in https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-87)

- Comparison with Spark: While its useful to compare against Scala version of Spark, I think we should also compare with PySpark which has a similar architecture. That would help us figure out where our overheads are in SparkR code vs. the architecture decisions

Thanks
Shivaram

Re: Have the ability to create and return a LabeledPoint RDD to be used with MLlib <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-131>

There is architectural issue on how to integrate the MLLIB into SparkR. In pySpark, py4j is used for bi-directional RPC between a jvm task and a python interpreter, so MLLIB can be called from Python. For SparkR, I can't find such a project that can serve such purpose. rJava allows R calls into Java in the same process, not inter-process. Maybe it is possible to use JRI to launch a in-process R engine within a jvm task, but not sure about the license issue (JRI is LGPL license) and not sure about the functional completeness of the R engine of JRI.
